items.us-sr::risk-based-governance: US banking organizations should maintain model risk management practices appropriate and effective for the risks they face, tailored to model risk (inherent risk in the context of a model's exposure and purpose) and to the size and complexity of their operations; the guidance is expected to be most relevant to organizations with over $30 billion in total assets and is non-prescriptive, so shortfalls do not themselves draw supervisory criticism, though supervisory action may follow unsafe or unsound practices stemming from insufficient model risk management. Generative and agentic AI models are outside the scope of this letter; its principles apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models.
items.us-sr::model-risk-assessment: Under SR 26-2, model risk is the potential for adverse financial consequences associated with models, including from decisions made based on model output. It is driven by a model's inherent risk - the assumptions, complexity, input quality and data constraints behind it - in the context of its materiality, which combines model exposure (the significance of model output to business decisions) and model purpose (including whether the model supports regulatory requirements or financial risk management). Sound practice assesses model risk both individually and in aggregate, accounting for interactions and dependencies among models and reliance on common assumptions, data or methodologies; models deemed immaterial may warrant only identification and monitoring of the conditions under which they could become material, while more material models warrant more comprehensive and rigorous oversight.
items.us-sr::model-validation: Under SR 26-2, model validation should occur before a model's first use, with its nature, rigor, and frequency aligned to the model's approach, use, and materiality; validation quality depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review rather than the organizational structure of the validation function, and should include outcomes analysis comparing model outputs with real-world outcomes, such as back-testing or outlier analysis. Urgent business need may justify earlier use only with controls, stakeholder information on limitations, and closer monitoring; ongoing monitoring should evaluate performance against potential changes in conditions.
items.us-sr::inventory-documentation: Under SR 26-2, all components of the model lifecycle benefit from model governance supported by clear policies and effective procedures that define risk management expectations and allocate resources commensurate with model risk and the organization's size and complexity; model risk management benefits from clearly delineated roles and responsibilities with well-defined accountability, including for potential conflicts of interest between reporting lines such as model development and validation, and for external resources used to manage model risk; it is sound practice to maintain a model inventory with sufficient information to understand model risks at the individual and aggregate levels, with detail reflecting model complexity and overall model usage, and adequate documentation, which supports continuity of operations, the tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions, and model remediation efforts.
items.us-sr::model-development-and-use: Under SR 26-2, sound model development is aligned with a model's purpose, business use, and banking organization policy, beginning with a clear statement of purpose that supports subsequent choices of data, methodologies, and testing approaches; developer judgment over conceptual design, inputs, assumptions, and methodology shapes the model's inherent risk. Input from model users and affected business managers strengthens model understanding and quality. Model testing - which may include out-of-sample and out-of-time testing, comparison of alternative assumptions and methodologies, and critical assessment of data quality - is a core component of development, with rigor commensurate with model complexity and materiality and potentially more limited for less material models or less complex organizations. Effective model use depends on understanding a model's limitations; using a model beyond its intended purpose adds uncertainty and risk, so extending a model's use warrants additional analysis of the new usage and its limitations and review of existing controls to manage the resulting risk.
items.us-sr::vendor-third-party: Under SR 26-2, customized vendor and other third-party products, including data, parameter values, or complete models, can present unique challenges for validation and other model risk management activities because proprietary components may withhold the underlying code, data, or methodology a bank would have for an internally developed model; nevertheless the principles of model risk management remain applicable. An important element is validation of vendor products, by internal or outside parties, including developing an understanding of the vendor model's conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance, and conducting ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to assess whether vendor models are accurate, remain fit for purpose, and continue to be reliable, which can also support any overlay or adjustment to model output; where vendor models are customized, sound practice involves appropriately documenting, justifying, and evaluating the customization adjustments as part of model validation.
